transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-04-05 16:00 UTC — Duration 58m; Recording: yes; Attendees listed above.

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations tailored to Hightower's cart/session flows. Discussed cost-sim scenarios, pilot sandbox, SOC2 + SSO questions, and actions to run a 2-week pilot.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we'll do a 15 minute walkthrough of the Optimize playbook then jump into the cost sims and sandbox plan.
[00:18] Laura (Hightower): Hi all, Laura here — heading ML at Hightower. We're focused on chat-assist for checkout and product Q/A. Latency matters for checkout paths.
[00:28] Diego (Redwood SE): Awesome. Quick note: we'll use the sessionization + prefix/KV cache patterns that map well to checkout flows — short prompt prefixes (cart context) repeated across requests.
[00:40] Omar (Hightower): We have fairly sticky sessions, many users make 3–6 calls per session. Average tokens per call about 80, per session ~240 tokens.
[00:54] Maya: Perfect, that aligns with our recommendations. We'll show sim numbers for a baseline hosted model and then tuned dedicated configs.
[01:05] Diego: First concept — batching tuning. For throughput you can increase batch window slightly and gain GPU efficiency. Example: at 8 concurrency and 40ms batch window we see about 3x throughput vs concurrency 1. But watch tail latency.
[01:30] Laura: We're worried about tail latency - checkout can't spike >300ms p95.
[01:37] Diego: Right — so we recommend an adaptive batching policy: target p50 under 120ms, permit batch growth only up to a p95 budget. Redwood Console lets you set latency SLOs per route and will fallback to a lower-latency variant if SLO breached.
[01:55] Maya: We'll put an example in the spreadsheet: baseline p50/p95, then simulated after batching changes and after adding prefix cache.
[02:08] Samir (Hightower): Can you explain the prefix/KV cache difference again? Our infra team confused "prefix cache" vs "KV session cache".
[02:18] Diego: Sure. Prefix cache stores the model's prefix KV states for repeated prompt prefixes — e.g., the cart summary that appears at start of each user request. On the other hand, KV session cache is session-level cached past tokens so you don't re-encode entire history. They overlap: prefix cache is a specialized, high-hit-rate store for short recurring contexts.
[02:38] Nina (Hightower): Any rough hit-rate we should expect?
[02:42] Diego: For cart flows we've seen 30–60% prefix hit-rate depending on how standardized the prompts are. If you canonicalize prompts (templated cart summaries) you can get to 55%+.
[02:55] Laura: Ok. What does that mean in cost terms?
[03:00] Maya: Quick numbers: baseline hosted cost example (hypothetical) — 1M tokens/month = $120 (for model tier X). With 35% prefix hit-rate + session KV hits you can see token delta drop by ~38% and GPU inference time reduce similarly, so unit cost reduction ~30–45% depending on batching.
[03:25] Diego: Another worked example in the sheet: 10k active sessions, avg 5 requests per session, avg 80 tokens per request. Baseline tokens = 4M tokens/day. If prefix hit-rate 40% and KV reuse 20% we project ~1.6M tokens/day avoided in full re-compute equivalence — that's large.
[03:47] Omar: Those numbers sound optimistic. How do you handle cold sessions/new cart templates?
[03:52] Diego: Combine strategies: lightweight LRU prefix cache for frequent templates + fallback to full model for cold. Also use prefetch (warm-up) on session start for accounts with high conversion probability — we can show a threshold rule in the playbook.
[04:09] Laura: What's prefetch cost vs savings?
[04:12] Diego: Prefetch is a small upfront cost. Example: prefetching 1 extra forward for 20% of sessions might add 0.2M tokens/day but enable cache hits on subsequent requests reducing much more. In sims often breaks even within a few requests.
[04:27] Maya: We'll add a break-even calculator in the spreadsheet so you can tweak prefetch fraction and view net tokens saved.
[04:35] Samir: On the enterprise side, we need KMS integration and audit logs. Is that supportable on Private?
[04:42] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integration, SSO/SAML, RBAC and exportable audit logs. We'll include SOC 2 docs. For audit retention you can choose log retention windows in the Console or ship to your ELK.
[04:58] Nina: Any latency impact when using KMS?
[05:02] Diego: Negligible at inference path if keys used for model artifacts aren't requested per invocation. Key exchange is during startup/deploy; runtime decryption is cached in memory. We'll document the threat model though.
[05:18] Maya: Back to cost models — we also cover quantization and model variant routing. For non-checkout flows you can route to a quantized smaller variant (4-bit) to save 40–60% cost with small quality delta.
[05:33] Laura: So routing policies could send checkout to full-precision, and FAQ/chat to quantized?
[05:38] Diego: Exactly. Redwood Optimize suggests routing by route and confidence thresholds.
[05:45] Omar: Show us a real sim for our peak 800 RPS scenario.
[05:49] Diego: Quick demo: opening the console (screen shared). [screen activity described]. We load the sandbox sim template pre-populated with your heatmap (sample). Here are three scenarios: baseline hosted, dedicated reserved with batching tuned, and private with prefix cache + prefetch.
[06:10] [screen share noises, mild cross talk]
[06:30] Diego: Baseline hosted: p50 86ms, p95 420ms at 800 RPS (not great for checkout p95). Dedicated w/ adaptive batching: p50 95ms, p95 220ms. Private w/ prefix cache enabled: p50 72ms, p95 160ms. Token-unit cost: baseline $0.12 per 1k tokens, dedicated tuned $0.085 per 1k tokens, private+cache effectively $0.044 per 1k tokens equivalent if hit-rates hold.
[07:05] Laura: Those per-1k-ballpark numbers are helpful. What assumptions on sequence length?
[07:09] Diego: These assume avg request 80 tokens, prompt prefix 30 tokens, KV reuse 20 tokens. We'll attach the sim assumptions in the sheet.
[07:20] Maya: Two tradeoffs to watch: higher batching reduces unit cost but can push tail latency; high prefix cache dependence has warm-up cold start concerns. Our recommended conservative starting config: batch window 25ms, concurrency cap 8, prefix TTL 30 minutes for cart summaries, LRU size pick based on top 10k templates.
[07:45] Samir: TTL 30 minutes seems arbitrary — can we do session-scoped TTL?
[07:49] Diego: Yes you can; Redwood supports session affinity TTL and policy-based eviction. For carts TTL per-user session is usually shorter (10–30m) but for account-level preferences you might want hours.
[08:02] Omar: About the sandbox pilot — what do you need from us?
[08:05] Maya: We'll need a small traffic sample, heatmap (peak windows), a representative prompt template set (top 50 templates), and target success criteria. Diego will provision the sandbox and run 3 scenarios over 48–72h.
[08:20] Nina: On security, our compliance requires SAML SSO and audit logs shipped to Splunk. Can Redwood push logs?
[08:26] Diego: Yes — Redwood can forward audit logs to your syslog/Splunk endpoint. We'll include the deployment checklist.
[08:35] [noise, pause]
[08:45] Maya: Quick notes on routing fallback — if dedicated capacity is saturated we can automatically fallback to hosted or a quantized variant to preserve availability. This avoids failed requests but may change cost and quality; we'll show threshold triggers.
[09:00] Laura: How do we measure quality regressions if we start using quantized variants?
[09:04] Diego: Redwood Optimize ties regressions to eval prompt sets — we recommend a small set of 100 critical prompts for checkout that we run for every rollout. Alerts trigger if similarity/accuracy drops beyond threshold.
[09:18] Samir: Any gotchas with caching around personalization tokens? We insert user-specific tokens in prompts — won't that break cache hit rates?
[09:27] Diego: Good point. Canonicalize prompts by replacing variable fields (user name, IDs) with placeholders before caching. The Console has a templating step to normalize prompts pre-cache. That drives up hit-rate.
[09:40] Omar: What's the expected engineering effort to onboard?
[09:43] Maya: For a pilot: 2 engineers part-time for 2 weeks to provide templates, heatmap and run tests. If you go Private with KMS/HSM, plan for 3-4 weeks (networking, certs, audit review).
[09:58] Laura: Pricing/contract — how does Redwood price the dedicated vs private?
[10:03] Maya: High level: hosted is usage-based per token. Dedicated has committed monthly capacity tiers (discounted) and options for burst. Private has platform fee + support + optional enterprise licensing. We'll send a tailored pricing summary in the follow-up.
[10:17] [Murmur]
[10:28] Diego: Back to sim specifics: here's a chart (described) showing cost vs latency for varying batch windows. At 15ms window we get moderate batching with p95 within budget; beyond 40ms gains diminish but p95 increases. So we recommend starting 20-30ms window.
[10:50] Laura: Are there built-in protections for request storms?
[10:54] Diego: Yes, rate-limiting and graceful degradation policies; you can specify route-level quotas and fallback targets. Also warm pool for sudden spikes.
[11:06] Omar: If we want to run a 2-week pilot, what's the minimal committed data we give you?
[11:10] Maya: Just a 48-72h sample first to validate sim assumptions and then full 2-week sandbox. Diego will run the first baseline sim within two business days of getting sample.
[11:20] [cross talk]
[11:34] Diego: One more technical note: KV cache storage choices — you can keep the cache in-process for fastest access on Dedicated/Private, or use a shared redis-backed store for multi-node clusters. In-process gives best latency but less cross-node sharing.
[11:52] Samir: For our global footprint, multi-region sync is a must. Does shared cache introduce extra network costs?
[11:58] Diego: Yes, cross-region cache fills add latency and cost. We recommend per-region prefix caches with eventual consistency for non-critical templates and route by region for lowest latency.
[12:12] Maya: Closing the demo: recap of next steps and owners (see action items). We'll send the cost spreadsheet, playbook link (https://redwood.example/playbooks/optimize-hightower — note placeholder), and SOC2 + SSO docs.
[12:28] Laura: Thanks, this was useful. We'll prioritize preparing the template list and heatmap.
[12:33] Maya: Great. Any final Qs?
[12:36] Nina: One last ask: can you include a short checklist for prompt canonicalization best practices?
[12:40] Diego: Yes, will include a 1-page checklist in the playbook.
[12:44] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and get the sandbox scheduled.
[12:50] [meeting ends, small chatter continues]

Notes on artifacts referenced: cost-simulation spreadsheet (link above, placeholder), Optimize playbook PDF, sandbox template (Console link), SOC2 and security checklist.

End of transcript.
